topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

outline.topic: Binary Logic in the Towers of Hanoi
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Language of Binary
sections.content: Briefly introduce binary as a base-2 system. Explain that just as decimal uses 10 digits (0-9), binary uses only 0 and 1, where each position represents a power of 2. Emphasize that every number can be uniquely expressed as a sum of powers of 2.
sections.example: Visual: A row of lightbulbs. 'Off' = 0, 'On' = 1. The number 5 is represented as 101 (1×2² + 0×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 4 + 0 + 1).

sections.title: Introduction to Towers of Hanoi
sections.content: Present the classic puzzle: 3 rods and N disks of different sizes. Rules: 1. Move one disk at a time. 2. A larger disk cannot be placed on a smaller one. Goal: Move the entire stack from Rod A to Rod C.
sections.example: Animation: A cute robot 'Robo-Disc' trying to move 3 disks while adhering to the 'no-large-on-small' rule.

sections.title: The Binary Connection: Identifying the Move
sections.content: Explain that the sequence of moves in the Towers of Hanoi corresponds directly to binary counting. To determine which disk to move at step 'n', look at the binary representation of 'n'. The position of the rightmost '1' bit indicates which disk to move (e.g., 1st bit = smallest disk, 2nd bit = second smallest, etc.).
sections.example: Table visualization: Step 1 (001) moves Disk 1; Step 2 (010) moves Disk 2; Step 3 (011) moves Disk 1 again. The animation shows the disks shifting in sync with the binary counter.

sections.title: Application: Predicting the Path
sections.content: Demonstrate that the total number of moves for N disks is 2^N - 1. This connects the geometric growth of the puzzle to the properties of binary numbers.
sections.example: Graphic: A progress bar labeled '2^N - 1'. For 3 disks, 2³ - 1 = 7 steps. The animation shows 7 binary increments leading exactly to the completion of the puzzle.

sections.title: Conclusion: Beyond the Puzzle
sections.content: Summarize that binary isn't just for counting—it’s a map for complex recursive processes. Encouraging the audience to see binary as the hidden 'DNA' behind algorithmic efficiency.
sections.example: Final visual: A DNA strand where each gene is a '0' or '1', transforming into the Towers of Hanoi, showing how simple bits encode complex movement patterns.

lecture_lines: The rightmost one indicates the disk.

lecture_lines: Total moves equals two to power N.
Subtract one for the exact count.
Three disks mean seven total steps.
